m2-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Working with chat assistants: getting real work done”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Treat the chat as a workbench with a boundary
sections.explanation: Messages, files and optional tools supply different inputs. Not every assistant has the same features or permissions.

items.label: Instructions
items.detail: State the task, reader and expected response.

items.label: Source material
items.detail: Supply only authorised files or excerpts needed for the task.

items.label: Available tools
items.detail: Check search, analysis and action permissions before relying on them.

items.label: Review surface
items.detail: Inspect the answer and any real sources or generated artefacts.

sections.takeaway: Inspect what is actually enabled rather than assuming the chat can see your files or access live information.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. The chat window is more than a text box

sections.title: Keep a conversation coherent
sections.explanation: A clean task thread makes assumptions easier to inspect. A long conversation is not a reliable permanent knowledge store.

items.label: Set a scope
items.detail: Give one task a clear purpose and evidence boundary.

items.label: Watch drift
items.detail: Notice conflicting instructions or irrelevant earlier material.

items.label: Summarise verified facts
items.detail: Keep a short working brief with sources and unresolved questions.

items.label: Restart deliberately
items.detail: Use a fresh thread when the task changes substantially.

sections.takeaway: Carry forward an explicit verified brief when you restart, rather than relying on implied memory.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Supply what the assistant cannot know
sections.explanation: Local requirements must come from authorised material or an identified person, not the model’s confidence.

items.label: Name the gap
items.detail: Identify the local fact or constraint the task needs.

items.label: Provide evidence
items.detail: Attach a permitted excerpt with its date and provenance.

items.label: Set a boundary
items.detail: Ask for answers only from that material and allow “not stated”.

items.label: Verify a citation
items.detail: Check that the quoted passage supports the exact claim.

sections.takeaway: If the source does not state an answer, leave it unknown rather than invent a plausible detail.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Giving the assistant what it cannot know

sections.title: Use an evidence log, not a brand contest
sections.explanation: The same evaluation rule makes assistant comparisons reproducible. Tool settings and availability can still differ.

items.label: Controlled input
items.detail: Use the same task and authorised source package.

items.label: Scored output
items.detail: Check the result using the same requirements and examples.

items.label: Recorded limitations
items.detail: Note missing features, failures and the conditions of the test.

sections.takeaway: Keep both successful and failed attempts so the comparison does not become cherry-picked marketing.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Replace weak habits with explicit decisions
sections.explanation: Repeatedly asking for “better” gives little information about what is wrong. Diagnosis makes revision more useful.

items.label: Find the failure
items.detail: Name the missing fact, wrong audience or broken constraint.

items.label: Give a focused fix
items.detail: Specify one change and keep the useful parts.

items.label: Recheck affected parts
items.detail: A revision can introduce a new error elsewhere.

items.label: Save the learning
items.detail: Record the improved brief and the check it still needs.

sections.takeaway: Do not paste more sensitive material or add grander role claims as a substitute for a clear brief.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Five habits that make output worse

checkpoint.question: What makes a comparison between two assistants defensible?
checkpoint.answer: Use the same task and authorised inputs, apply the same checks, and record failures and settings as well as the preferred result.

m2-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Prompt anatomy: RTF and CO-STAR”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A brief is a set of choices, not a magic phrase
sections.explanation: The six building blocks answer different questions. Select the ones the task needs instead of making every prompt longer.

items.label: Role
items.detail: Describe a useful perspective without treating the model as a licensed professional.

items.label: Context
items.detail: Provide the relevant situation and authorised background.

items.label: Task
items.detail: Name the exact work to be done.

items.label: Constraints
items.detail: Set evidence, length, safety and scope boundaries.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Specify the output structure the reader can use.

items.label: Examples
items.detail: Show a permitted example of the expected result.

sections.takeaway: A role description cannot supply missing facts, permission or verification.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: RTF is a compact starting point
sections.explanation: Role, Task and Format are enough to structure many small, easy-to-check requests.

items.label: Role
items.detail: A careful editor for Indian college writing is a useful perspective.

items.label: Task
items.detail: Tighten grammar without changing the author’s meaning or voice.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Ask for the revised paragraph and a short change list.

sections.takeaway: Use an appropriately small brief, then still inspect whether meaning changed.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Make the CO-STAR components visible
sections.explanation: Switch a component off and inspect what disappears. This assembles instructions; it does not generate an answer or score a model.

items.label: Context
items.detail: Give the situation the assistant cannot know.
items.example: Fictional practice: a Mysuru college placement team is planning an alumni mentoring session. The date and venue are not yet approved.

items.label: Objective
items.detail: Describe the reader’s intended next action.
items.example: Draft an invitation asking alumni to indicate interest through [RSVP LINK]. Do not imply the event is confirmed.

items.label: Style
items.detail: Choose the form of writing, not the emotional register.
items.example: Use clear Indian English, short paragraphs and a meaningful subject line. Avoid promotional jargon.

items.label: Tone
items.detail: Set the emotional register for the relationship.
items.example: Warm, respectful and concise. Do not use pressure or exaggerated promises.

items.label: Audience
items.detail: Name the reader and relevant knowledge.
items.example: Alumni who may volunteer as mentors; assume no prior knowledge of this proposed session.

items.label: Response
items.detail: Specify format and include an evidence boundary.
items.example: Return a subject line and an email under 160 words. Use [DATE TO CONFIRM] and [VENUE TO CONFIRM]; never invent event details.

sections.takeaway: Even all six components do not guarantee a factual or safe response. Verify the result against the real evidence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Diagnose before asking for another draft
sections.explanation: A revision should target a named weakness while protecting parts already checked.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: Name the factual, structural or audience mismatch.

items.label: Direct a fix
items.detail: Request a concrete change rather than “make it better”.

items.label: Lock what works
items.detail: Protect verified sections that do not need revision.

items.label: Test and save
items.detail: Recheck the response and keep the final reusable brief.

sections.takeaway: A changed prompt is a hypothesis about improvement, not evidence that the new output is correct.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Small boundaries prevent large misunderstandings
sections.explanation: Delimiters, placeholders and precise output instructions help separate the task from the material being analysed.

items.label: Mark source material
items.detail: Use clear headings to distinguish evidence from instructions.

items.label: Permit uncertainty
items.detail: Request a visible placeholder when a necessary fact is missing.

items.label: Specify the result
items.detail: Name the reader, length and output structure explicitly.

items.label: Review meaning
items.detail: Check that the response follows the evidence as well as the format.

sections.takeaway: A delimiter is a formatting aid, not a security boundary against malicious source instructions.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does “6 of 6 brief parts included” mean that the answer will be correct?
checkpoint.answer: No. It reports which instructions are present. It is not a quality score, an AI evaluation or a substitute for checking facts.

m2-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Advanced prompting patterns”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Examples teach a pattern, including its mistakes
sections.explanation: Few-shot prompting supplies examples of the desired mapping. The examples must be permitted, consistent and relevant.

items.label: Choose examples
items.detail: Use representative, safe input/output pairs.

items.label: Show the rule
items.detail: Keep labels and formatting consistent across pairs.

items.label: Add a new case
items.detail: Test a case that is different enough to expose overfitting.

items.label: Verify the mapping
items.detail: Check the answer independently against the intended rule.

sections.takeaway: Do not use private records or misleading examples to teach a convenient but wrong pattern.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Request inspectable working, then check it
sections.explanation: For a calculation or classification, ask for the relevant assumptions, method and checkable result. A generated explanation is not proof of internal reasoning.

items.label: State the inputs
items.detail: Provide a clearly bounded problem and known values.

items.label: Request a method
items.detail: Ask for concise, checkable steps or a calculation table.

items.label: Test a step
items.detail: Independently reproduce a material intermediate result.

items.label: Check the conclusion
items.detail: Verify that the final claim follows from the stated inputs.

sections.takeaway: Do not treat verbose reasoning as verification; reproduce the crucial calculation or consult evidence yourself.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: Pattern 2 — Step-by-step reasoning ("think before you answer")

sections.title: Step back to the principle before the case
sections.explanation: A broad principle can organise a messy request, but the principle must fit the actual case.

items.label: Name the case
items.detail: Describe the real problem without extra assumptions.

items.label: Identify the principle
items.detail: Ask which concept or framework is relevant.

items.label: Apply cautiously
items.detail: Map the principle onto the supplied facts.

items.label: Check the fit
items.detail: Look for exceptions or facts the abstraction leaves out.

sections.takeaway: Return to the specific evidence before recommending action.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A persona panel is a rehearsal, not research
sections.explanation: Simulated perspectives can reveal questions to investigate. They are not interviews with customers or affected people.

items.label: Different concerns
items.detail: Ask fictional perspectives to raise different objections.

items.label: Shared evidence
items.detail: Give every perspective the same known facts and limitations.

items.label: Real follow-up
items.detail: Turn objections into questions for actual users or reviewers.

sections.takeaway: Label synthetic voices and validate important assumptions with real authorised evidence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Critique needs an external standard
sections.explanation: Self-critique can improve a draft when there is an explicit rubric, but one model can repeat or defend its own error.

items.label: Set criteria
items.detail: Define what correctness, completeness and clarity mean.

items.label: Inspect the draft
items.detail: Ask for specific mismatches with those criteria.

items.label: Revise selectively
items.detail: Change the affected parts without inventing evidence.

items.label: Check independently
items.detail: Reproduce a calculation or open an authoritative source.

sections.takeaway: Verify important factual claims independently, including in the revised answer.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A template constrains shape, not truth
sections.explanation: An output template helps another person or workflow consume the answer. It cannot guarantee valid content.

items.label: Specify fields
items.detail: Name required labels and allowed values.

items.label: Allow unknowns
items.detail: Provide an honest representation for missing information.

items.label: Validate shape
items.detail: Check required fields and formatting rules.

items.label: Validate meaning
items.detail: Check that every value is supported by the source.

sections.takeaway: Validate both the structure and the meaning before accepting a formatted result.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A chain needs checks between links
sections.explanation: Breaking a task into stages exposes intermediate artefacts. An unchecked early mistake can otherwise flow into every later stage.

items.label: Gather evidence
items.detail: Collect permitted material with provenance.

items.label: Produce an intermediate
items.detail: Create a summary or outline tied to that material.

items.label: Review the hand-off
items.detail: Check accuracy and approval before the next step.

items.label: Build the final
items.detail: Use the verified intermediate and check the final result.

sections.takeaway: Keep source references through the chain and pause before an external or irreversible action.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Match the pattern to the failure
sections.explanation: Different patterns solve different communication problems. Use the simplest one that addresses the observed weakness.

items.label: Wrong shape
items.detail: Use a small template or relevant example.

items.label: Weak structure
items.detail: Try an outline or a staged workflow.

items.label: Missing perspectives
items.detail: Use a clearly labelled rehearsal panel to generate questions.

items.label: Wrong facts
items.detail: Supply better evidence and verify; prompt decoration cannot create truth.

sections.takeaway: More patterns and longer prompts do not automatically improve a response.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Stop when complexity hides the task
sections.explanation: A complicated prompt can introduce contradictions, cost and unnecessary context. Compare the result against a simpler baseline.

items.label: Keep a baseline
items.detail: Save the simplest workable brief and output.

items.label: Change one thing
items.detail: Add a pattern to address one diagnosed weakness.

items.label: Compare fairly
items.detail: Use the same criteria and test cases.

items.label: Keep or remove
items.detail: Retain the change only when the evidence supports it.

sections.takeaway: Discard a pattern that does not improve a relevant, independently checked outcome.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does a simulated customer panel count as real customer validation?
checkpoint.answer: No. It can generate questions, but it must be labelled synthetic and followed by real, authorised user evidence when validation is required.

m2-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “Prompting for your discipline”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Commerce prompts need source and calculation checks
sections.explanation: Use AI to structure an explanation or a working table, not as the authority for a tax, legal or accounting conclusion.

items.label: Define the case
items.detail: Use synthetic or authorised figures and state the accounting question.

items.label: Specify a method
items.detail: Request assumptions, units and checkable workings.

items.label: Reproduce results
items.detail: Recalculate totals and inspect the applicable rule source.

items.label: Review before use
items.detail: Keep specialist decisions with an authorised qualified person.

sections.takeaway: Verify applicable rules with current authoritative material and seek qualified review where needed.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Management drafts need a real audience and evidence
sections.explanation: A proposed campaign or HR message is useful only when it fits its audience, permissions and actual inputs.

items.label: Set the decision
items.detail: State which action the reader will consider.

items.label: Supply evidence
items.detail: Use approved research, product facts or synthetic cases.

items.label: Draft options
items.detail: Ask for alternatives and explicit assumptions.

items.label: Check consequences
items.detail: Review claims, fairness, rights and practical constraints.

sections.takeaway: Do not turn invented market research, employee claims or forecast results into business evidence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Use an arts assistant without losing the source
sections.explanation: A writing or humanities task needs a visible boundary between source, interpretation and your own argument.

items.label: Read the source
items.detail: Know the passage or evidence before asking for help.

items.label: Ask a bounded question
items.detail: Request comparison, structure or critique tied to the passage.

items.label: Check quotations
items.detail: Find each quotation and citation in the original.

items.label: Write your argument
items.detail: Credit assistance without outsourcing the judgement.

sections.takeaway: An invented quote or reference remains false even when its prose is elegant.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Science prompts need units, method and uncertainty
sections.explanation: A scientific explanation or calculation must remain reproducible and consistent with the supplied evidence.

items.label: State inputs
items.detail: Name quantities, units and experimental conditions.

items.label: Ask for a method
items.detail: Request a checkable calculation or explanation.

items.label: Test independently
items.detail: Check units, plausibility and a calculation by hand.

items.label: Report limits
items.detail: Separate measured values from hypotheses and unknowns.

sections.takeaway: Never invent observations or lab results to complete an attractive report.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Bilingual quality needs a meaning check
sections.explanation: Translation quality depends on meaning, terminology and the audience—not merely whether the output is in another script.

items.label: Define the reader
items.detail: State language, reading level and desired register.

items.label: Keep terminology
items.detail: Supply a short approved glossary for key terms.

items.label: Compare meanings
items.detail: Review omissions, numbers, names and tone across languages.

items.label: Revise and approve
items.detail: Have an appropriate speaker check the final message.

sections.takeaway: Use a fluent reviewer for important communication and retain the original meaning through revisions.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: What must a science learner do if an assistant supplies plausible experimental results that were never observed?
checkpoint.answer: Reject them as fabricated evidence. Use actual authorised observations or clearly labelled synthetic practice data, and document what is unknown.

m2-t5.introduction: A second way to understand “Research & writing assistants”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Research tools have different evidence boundaries
sections.explanation: A general assistant, a source-search tool and a notebook can all help with research, but none removes your responsibility to inspect sources.

items.label: General chat
items.detail: Useful for questions and structure; it can invent references.

items.label: Search-oriented tool
items.detail: Can retrieve sources, whose relevance and authority still need review.

items.label: Source notebook
items.detail: Works with a chosen document set; its summaries and quotations still need checking.

sections.takeaway: A citation icon is a starting point for verification, not a guarantee that the claim is supported.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Keep a research trail from question to claim
sections.explanation: A defensible summary lets a reader trace each important claim back to the underlying material.

items.label: Frame the question
items.detail: Set scope, time period and evidence needs.

items.label: Find and open
items.detail: Inspect primary material rather than only search snippets.

items.label: Extract with provenance
items.detail: Record the passage, source and relevant limitation.

items.label: Synthesize and check
items.detail: Write the conclusion and verify every material claim.

sections.takeaway: Record missing or conflicting evidence rather than smoothing it into a single confident conclusion.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. A research workflow that survives scrutiny

sections.title: Grounded notebooks still need source inspection
sections.explanation: A notebook reduces the evidence scope, but extraction and interpretation can still go wrong.

items.label: Curate sources
items.detail: Use relevant authorised documents and identify their versions.

items.label: Ask a bounded question
items.detail: State that answers must stay within the source set.

items.label: Open the passage
items.detail: Check the cited location and the surrounding context.

items.label: Correct the summary
items.detail: Fix unsupported statements and preserve uncertainty.

sections.takeaway: If the source does not contain the answer, “not stated” is preferable to a plausible completion.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Getting the most from a notebook tool

sections.title: A long research report can scale an error
sections.explanation: Automated research can collect more material quickly, which increases the need for sampling and claim checks.

items.label: Set a brief
items.detail: Define the question and acceptable source types.

items.label: Review the plan
items.detail: Check whether the search is likely to answer the right question.

items.label: Audit findings
items.detail: Open consequential and surprising claims in their sources.

items.label: Keep a limitations note
items.detail: State what was not covered and what remains unresolved.

sections.takeaway: Length and number of links do not establish source quality or factual completeness.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Cite the material you actually used
sections.explanation: Citation is a traceability practice. It should identify a real source that you opened and that supports the specific claim.

items.label: Open the original
items.detail: Confirm the source exists and inspect the relevant passage.

items.label: Check metadata
items.detail: Verify author, title, date and location rather than copying a generated citation.

items.label: Link the claim
items.detail: Make sure the source supports that sentence, not only the topic.

items.label: Credit assistance
items.detail: Follow the task’s AI-use and referencing policy.

sections.takeaway: Disclose AI assistance separately from crediting the underlying evidence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can you cite a paper you have only seen as an assistant-generated reference?
checkpoint.answer: No. Locate and open the actual source, verify its metadata and supporting passage, then cite the material you really used.

m2-t6.introduction: A second way to understand “Evaluating & refining GenAI outputs”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A short fact check should prioritise consequence
sections.explanation: Check the claims that would materially change the reader’s decision. A quick routine is a triage method, not certification of every sentence.

items.label: Extract claims
items.detail: Identify names, dates, figures, quotations and recommendations.

items.label: Rank consequence
items.detail: Prioritise what would cause harm or change a decision if wrong.

items.label: Verify independently
items.detail: Use an authoritative source or reproduce the calculation.

items.label: Document uncertainty
items.detail: Record the unsupported point and the effect on the conclusion.

sections.takeaway: If an important claim cannot be checked, qualify or remove it rather than rely on confident wording.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Use the same rubric on every candidate
sections.explanation: The five criteria make an output easier to inspect, but a high average must not conceal a material falsehood.

items.label: Correct
items.detail: Facts and calculations match evidence.

items.label: Complete
items.detail: The required parts of the task are present.

items.label: Constraint-compliant
items.detail: Scope, length, format and safety limits are followed.

items.label: Clear
items.detail: The intended reader can understand and use it.

items.label: Credible
items.detail: Claims are traceable and uncertainty is explicit.

sections.takeaway: Treat a serious correctness or safety failure as a reason to stop, not a score to average away.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. A rubric you can use on anything

sections.title: Writing style is not an AI detector
sections.explanation: Generic phrasing can be a reason to improve writing. It is not reliable evidence of authorship or factual error on its own.

items.label: Stylistic signal
items.detail: Repetition or vague language can weaken a piece.

items.label: Substantive check
items.detail: Inspect evidence, correctness and concrete meaning.

items.label: Revision goal
items.detail: Make the writing specific and useful without fabricating details.

sections.takeaway: Evaluate substance and provenance; do not accuse someone based only on style.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A/B testing needs a fixed question
sections.explanation: Changing one prompt element helps attribute a difference in the tested outputs. Multiple runs and a fixed rubric reduce cherry-picking.

items.label: Keep a baseline
items.detail: Use a known task, evidence package and evaluation rule.

items.label: Change one factor
items.detail: Alter the specific instruction you want to test.

items.label: Run and compare
items.detail: Record successes and failures under consistent conditions.

items.label: Retest a choice
items.detail: Try different relevant cases before saving the change.

sections.takeaway: A favourable small test does not prove that the prompt always works.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A prompt library is an evidence library
sections.explanation: A reusable prompt should carry its purpose, limits and checks rather than only its wording.

items.label: Name the trigger
items.detail: State when the prompt is useful and when it is not.

items.label: Store the brief
items.detail: Keep a clear input template without private data.

items.label: Attach evidence
items.detail: Link example results, failed cases and review notes.

items.label: Version the entry
items.detail: Record a change and its required verification step.

sections.takeaway: Revalidate stored prompts when the task, tool or source requirements change.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a strong average rubric score outweigh a fabricated source in the answer?
checkpoint.answer: No. A material falsehood or safety failure needs correction or rejection; it must not be averaged away by good formatting or clarity.

m2-pb1.introduction: A second way to understand “Project Block 1 — Personal Prompt Playbook”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Personal Prompt Playbook: from purpose to evidence
sections.explanation: Ten reusable prompts for actual degree or career tasks, each tested and independently checked.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: Ten reusable prompts for actual degree or career tasks, each tested and independently checked.

items.label: Build an artefact
items.detail: Create the required work for the stated audience and scope.

items.label: Verify and explain
items.detail: Keep test evidence, permissions, limitations and your contribution.

sections.takeaway: Use the full original brief for requirements, timing and marks; this diagram is a companion, not a replacement.

sections.title: Organise the personal prompt playbook evidence pack
sections.explanation: Group the required files so a reviewer can inspect the work and its checks. The detailed checklist above remains unchanged.

items.label: Ten tested entries
items.detail: Include each trigger, final brief, patterns, tool choice, example and version note.

items.label: Prompt chain
items.detail: Show one substantial chain; it counts as at most three of the ten entries.

items.label: Bilingual example

items.label: Evidence log

items.label: Reflection

items.label: Cover and disclosure

sections.takeaway: Reading the brief is not submission, external project marking or facilitator approval.

sections.title: Ten prompts need breadth as well as polish
sections.explanation: The original coverage allocates ten prompt purposes. Keep the task choice tied to your degree and goal.

items.label: Produce · 3
items.detail: Draft useful material and show the relevant output check.

items.label: Analyse · 2
items.detail: Compare or calculate with independently checkable evidence.

items.label: Learn · 2
items.detail: Use explanations or practice that you can assess.

items.label: Communicate · 1
items.detail: Serve a non-expert or community audience.

items.label: Critique · 1
items.detail: Apply a relevant panel or rubric with verification.

items.label: Your goal · 1

sections.takeaway: A prompt chain can count as up to three entries, not ten additional entries; retain the original counting rules.

sections.title: Plan, build, check and revise
sections.explanation: Use the original suggested schedule to reserve time for review rather than doing all the checking after the final export.

items.label: Plan the scope
items.detail: Start from the actual brief, required outputs and permitted inputs.

items.label: Build deliberately
items.detail: Work in small versions and retain intermediate artefacts.

items.label: Review evidence
items.detail: Run the relevant source, language, functionality and safety checks.

checkpoint.question: Can ten unchanged prompts copied from the lessons demonstrate your own playbook quality?
checkpoint.answer: No. Adapt them to your actual tasks, test them, record checks and explain the changes. Follow the complete original submission and coverage rules.
